title: Carmichael's λ(n) sharpens Euler's exponent
content: Euler's theorem gives a^φ(n) = 1 for every unit a of ZMod n, so every unit's order divides φ(n) (the parent's orderOf_dvd_totient). But φ(n) is usually not the smallest exponent annihilating all units at once. The least such 'universal exponent' is Carmichael's function λ(n), defined here as the group exponent of (ZMod n)ˣ. This entry answers the parent's open question by proving λ(n) is the exact least universal exponent, that λ(n) ∣ φ(n), and — at n = 8 — that the inequality λ(8) = 2 < 4 = φ(8) is strict, so Euler's exponent is genuinely non-minimal.
mathContext: $a^{\varphi(n)} = 1$ for all units (Euler), but $\lambda(n) = \exp\big((\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times\big) \mid \varphi(n)$ is the least exponent with $a^{\lambda(n)} = 1$.

title: λ(n) := exponent of (ZMod n)ˣ
content: Carmichael's function is defined as the monoid/group exponent of the unit group (ZMod n)ˣ — the smallest N with a^N = 1 for every unit a. Defining λ(n) directly as Monoid.exponent lets every property below be inherited from Mathlib's general exponent API rather than reproved from scratch; the 'least exponent' characterization is then a theorem (carmichael_isLeast), not part of the definition.

title: λ(n) is a universal exponent
content: Every unit is annihilated by λ(n): a^λ(n) = 1. This is Euler's a^φ(n) = 1 with φ(n) replaced by the possibly-smaller λ(n), and follows immediately from Monoid.pow_exponent_eq_one applied to the definition.

title: The universal exponents are exactly the multiples of λ(n)
content: λ(n) ∣ N if and only if a^N = 1 for every unit a. This bidirectional statement pins down the whole set of universal exponents as the ideal (multiples) of λ(n) in ℕ — the structural fact behind both minimality and the divisibility λ(n) ∣ φ(n).

title: λ(n) is the least universal exponent (headline)
content: The main sharpening: among all positive N with a^N = 1 for every unit a, λ(n) is the minimum. It is itself such an exponent (positivity via carmichael_pos, annihilation via pow_carmichael), and it divides — hence is ≤ — any other, using Nat.le_of_dvd with carmichael_dvd_iff. This is the exact converse-refinement the parent left open: it upgrades 'orderOf u ∣ φ(n)' to a genuine minimality statement.

title: Every unit's order divides λ(n)
content: The multiplicative order of any unit divides λ(n) (Monoid.order_dvd_exponent). Chained with λ(n) ∣ φ(n) below, this recovers the parent's orderOf u ∣ φ(n) as the composite ord(a) ∣ λ(n) ∣ φ(n) — exhibiting λ as the intermediate, sharper divisor.

title: λ(n) ∣ φ(n): the refinement
content: Carmichael's exponent divides Euler's, because the exponent of any finite group divides its order (Group.exponent_dvd_card), and |(ZMod n)ˣ| = φ(n) (ZMod.card_units_eq_totient). This divisibility is what makes λ a refinement of φ rather than an unrelated quantity, and orderOf_dvd_totient then factors the parent divisibility through λ: ord(a) ∣ λ(n) ∣ φ(n).

title: Agreement with Mathlib's Carmichael function
content: The locally-defined λ(n) coincides with Mathlib's official ArithmeticFunction.Carmichael for n ≠ 0, via ArithmeticFunction.carmichael_eq_exponent'. This bridges the exponent-based definition used here to the standard number-theoretic arithmetic function, ensuring results transfer.

title: The gap at n = 8
content: The concrete witness that φ is not sharp. The unit group (ZMod 8)ˣ ≅ ℤ/2 × ℤ/2 is elementary abelian of exponent 2 — every unit already squares to 1 — even though it has order 4. So λ(8) = 2 while φ(8) = 4. This is the smallest n exhibiting a strict gap λ(n) < φ(n).

title: Computing λ(8) = 2
content: λ(8) = 2 is squeezed between an upper and lower bound. Upper: sq_eq_one_zmod_eight (a decide over the four units) gives a² = 1 for all units, so λ(8) ∣ 2, hence λ(8) ≤ 2. Lower: some unit (e.g. 3) is not the identity, so λ(8) ≠ 1 (an exponent-1 group would be trivial). With 0 < λ(8) ≤ 2 and λ(8) ≠ 1, omega concludes λ(8) = 2. All finite checks use decide, not native_decide, so no Lean.ofReduceBool dependency.

title: Euler's exponent is not minimal
content: The punchline: at n = 8 the exponent N = 2 is positive, strictly below φ(8) = 4, and already annihilates every unit. So φ(n) from Euler's theorem is not in general the least universal exponent — Carmichael's λ(8) = 2 is the sharp replacement. This concretely demonstrates that the minimality proved abstractly in carmichael_isLeast is a genuine improvement over Euler's bound.
